title: Know Your Attack Surface: Discovery and Port Scanning with nmap
intro: Attackers scan the whole internet continuously, so anything you expose will be found within hours. Defenders scan their own networks first, to find what's exposed before someone else does. Only ever scan networks you own or are explicitly authorised to test: unauthorised scanning is illegal in many countries and breaks most cloud providers' terms.

steps.prompt: Find which hosts are alive on your office server subnet 10.0.1.0/24, without port scanning them.
steps.fake_output:
Nmap scan report for 10.0.1.1
Host is up (0.00031s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.0.1.15
Host is up (0.00052s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.0.1.23
Host is up (0.00048s latency).
Nmap scan report for 10.0.1.77
Host is up (0.00061s latency).
Nmap done: 256 IP addresses (4 hosts up) scanned in 2.41 seconds
steps.explanation: Four live hosts. 10.0.1.77 isn't in your inventory.
steps.why: -sn is a 'ping sweep' (host discovery only): fast and low-noise. Comparing live hosts against your inventory (CMDB or cloud API) finds unknown machines, which are often forgotten test boxes or someone's shadow IT, and unmanaged machines are the ones that don't get patched.

steps.prompt: Scan the unknown host 10.0.1.77 for the 1000 most common TCP ports.
steps.fake_output:
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp   open     ssh
80/tcp   open     http
3306/tcp open     mysql
8080/tcp filtered http-proxy

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 4.12 seconds
steps.explanation: SSH, HTTP, and MySQL are open; 8080 is filtered.
steps.why: open means something answered; closed means the host replied 'nothing here' (RST); filtered means a firewall dropped the probe, the same 'timeout vs refused' distinction from the networking category. A database listening on a general server subnet is worth a question.

steps.prompt: The default scan misses non-standard ports. Scan all 65535 TCP ports on 10.0.1.77, faster timing (-T4).
steps.fake_output:
PORT      STATE SERVICE
22/tcp    open  ssh
80/tcp    open  http
3306/tcp  open  mysql
31337/tcp open  Elite

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 38.77 seconds
steps.explanation: Port 31337 is open, which the top-1000 scan missed. That port has a long history of being used by backdoors.
steps.why: The 'top 1000 ports' covers common services, but admins (and attackers) put things on odd ports all the time. A full-range scan is slower but is the only way to see everything that's listening.

steps.prompt: Some hosts drop ping, so nmap wrongly marks them 'down'. Scan host 10.0.1.90 skipping host discovery.
steps.fake_output:
PORT    STATE SERVICE
443/tcp open  https

Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 5.02 seconds
steps.explanation: 10.0.1.90 didn't answer the earlier ping sweep, but it's up and serving HTTPS.
steps.why: Cloud and hardened hosts often block ICMP, so a ping sweep undercounts. -Pn treats every target as up and scans it anyway. It's slower across large ranges, but it's how you avoid missing firewalled hosts.

steps.prompt: Save a full scan of 10.0.1.0/24 in all output formats with basename scan-2026-09-28, for comparison next week.
steps.fake_output:
Nmap done: 256 IP addresses (5 hosts up) scanned in 22.9 seconds
(written: scan-2026-09-28.nmap, scan-2026-09-28.xml, scan-2026-09-28.gnmap)
steps.explanation: Normal, XML, and grepable output saved.
steps.why: One scan is a snapshot; the value is in the difference over time. 'ndiff old.xml new.xml' shows newly opened ports, which usually means a new service or a mistake. Mature teams run this on a schedule and alert on changes.
